stem:
A woman at 16 weeks is diagnosed with secondary syphilis after a new rash and confirmatory serology. She has no penicillin allergy and no neurological or ocular symptoms. The antenatal team has arranged urgent sexual-health specialist involvement.

Which antibiotic is the appropriate basis of treatment?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Long-acting IM benzathine benzylpenicillin treats early syphilis in pregnancy. The specialist team coordinates dosing and follow-up, and counsels about a possible Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction after treatment.

options.label: B
options.text: Oral doxycycline twice daily for 14 days
options.explanation: A 14-day doxycycline course is an alternative for early syphilis in selected nonpregnant adults, but tetracyclines are avoided in pregnancy and it does not substitute for penicillin here.

options.label: C
options.text: Oral azithromycin as a single 2 g dose
options.explanation: Macrolide resistance and unreliable prevention of congenital infection make azithromycin unsuitable as the standard treatment in this setting.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Oral amoxicillin with probenecid is not the recommended early-syphilis regimen in pregnancy. The sustained exposure supplied by long-acting benzathine benzylpenicillin is what matters.

options.label: E
options.explanation: IV benzylpenicillin is used for neurosyphilis and certain other specialist indications. With uncomplicated secondary disease and no neurological or ocular features, the routine regimen is benzathine benzylpenicillin IM.

context: Early syphilis in pregnancy is treated with intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin with urgent specialist coordination.
